title: What is expected from her.
paragraphs: My parents talk about doing their jobs well and taking care of their family. My mom looks after the older and younger people; my second aunt thinks she has to keep learning to meet expectations at work. My first aunt says she has less family and my grandma says she is not under pressure now. I see that expectations are based on the role each woman has at work and her age. What was once expected of my grandma may now be part of my mom’s everyday life, though I would have to ask more about how this changed.

title: What makes a day her own.
paragraphs: All four women speak about ordinary life with family: making dinner, sharing a meal, talking, or keeping healthy. It seems to be that people from generations, who are very close to one another, care about each other. And that makes me think about “making room for others” in a different way. Family can be a pleasure for a woman, or it can be something expected of her. I still want to know when she has time for herself, and whether she feels she needs a reason to take it.

title: Who she makes room for.
paragraphs: My mom puts her children first. My grandma thinks of us all, and both my aunts want their family to be healthy and safe. What I find in their answers is that so much of what matters to them also comes from people. This is related to the notion that women should care and be considerate, but I don’t want to assume their love is just something they have learned to be. I want to have a picture of what their own wishes are and not just the ones for the people they care about.

title: What she would have done differently.
paragraphs: My grandma regrets marrying and leaving her village. Both my aunts would study hard, and my first aunt would stay in her first job. These answers are why I think of how each woman looks back at the choices she had. Education and work can help you choose a direction, marriage and care can change where that direction leads. Across generations, being happy now does not mean that an earlier wish has stopped mattering. Regret also doesn’t mean she loves her family any less.

The interviews provoke me to consider how expectations change in a woman’s life. But their answers don’t tell me much about being a “good girl” or being judged on the basis of their appearance. I would need to get to know about those experiences before connecting them to the interviews. And I don’t want to see each woman as representing a whole generation. Their ages matter, but so do their work, relationships and choices they have made.

title: What she takes care of.
paragraphs: My mom says she decides the little things at home and Dad decides the big things, but there are hardly any big things. I wonder who gets to decide and who actually does the everyday work. Xiao Min takes care of the big things and says she is happy to do them within her abilities. Zheng Juan also feels she can do the little things as long as she has the energy. Xiao Sheng says her family expects her to do the housework, but she thinks everyone should share it. Fang Hanqin is the one taking care of family and social relationships and communicating with the children’s school. She feels more at ease doing things herself. I wonder how trusting her own way of doing things becomes part of the work she takes on. I observe different ways of accepting or questioning the work at home. Being willing to do something doesn’t tell me whether she could choose not to do it.

title: When she says no.
paragraphs: Both my mom and Xiao Sheng have said that they have wanted to refuse a family request and have said it. Fang Hanqin also says that there are things she refuses and that she says it out loud. They are short answers, and I still want to know what happened afterwards. Xiao Min says her parents do not ask anything of her and she often volunteers, but she says no when her children’s requests are unreasonable. Zheng Juan says her parents hardly ask anything of her. These answers make me think that expectations aren’t always expressed out loud. Someone could offer to help before anyone asks, but I don’t want to say she’s forced to. I want to know whether saying no changes what the family expects next time, and whether she has to explain herself.

title: What people might say.
paragraphs: My mom wanted a brighter hair colour but gave it up because she was afraid of what people would say. She also worried about getting a perm, but she thought it would be nice and did it anyway. I find this interesting because the same worry can lead to different choices. Xiao Min used to care about what people think of her and now she feels she can do what she thinks is right. Xiao Sheng also gave things up before, but later did what she wanted. Zheng Juan does not remember this worry and thinks it would not stop her. Fang Hanqin has both given things up because of possible comments and followed her heart even while worrying about them. I don’t look at these answers as one step from being afraid to being free. Sometimes the worry is still there when she goes ahead. I still want to know whose comments matter, and why one choice feels easier to make than another.

title: What happiness leaves room for.
paragraphs: My mom is happy that her parents are healthy, her children are doing well, and she is building a business with Dad. But she also wants a house she loves, where she can grow flowers and drink tea. I love that this wish shows me a picture of a life she wants for herself. Xiao Min talks about being free to be herself and how she hopes her sons will think differently about learning. Xiao Sheng finds happiness in her daughter and wishes her partner would change their bad temper. Zheng Juan says happiness can be a mood-driven thing and life sometimes feels tiring. Fang Hanqin describes happiness as something she feels in the moment: her family being safe, her children doing well, and progress in her career. She would like to be more open-minded and more at peace with things, and she hopes the energy around her might also get better. I notice that the change she wants is also in how she meets her life. Their answers make me believe that being happy and wanting something to change can happen together. I don’t want to read their care for family as leaving no room for their own wishes.

title: What living well means to her.
paragraphs: When my mom was young, a stable job and a good husband seemed enough. Now she thinks that a woman needs to be able to support herself. Xiao Sheng once wanted everybody to love her, but now she wants enough money and the right amount of love. Xiao Min still thinks of having money to spend and of looking beautiful, like she did as a kid. Zheng Juan still wants love and money, but now she also wants good looks and free time. Fang Hanqin still thinks a happy family, no debts, and financial freedom are the keys to living well. But her desire for material things has weakened with age, and she now views peace and good health as the greatest happiness. Her idea of it has stayed much the same, but what matters most in it seems to have changed. Some wishes change and some stay. I don’t think independence means that love doesn’t matter or that wanting to look beautiful tells me how much freedom a woman has. I want to know what each of them feels able to choose and what she needs to make that choice possible.
